title: Checkpoint: How Computers Came to Be
objective: After this level you can trace computing from punched cards to smartphones and name the switch that powered each era.
summary: Each era of computing ran on a switch: pins through punched holes, vacuum tubes, transistors, then transistors on chips. Recap of cards, Lovelace, Turing, ENIAC, stored programs and the PC.

cards.headline: Holes, tubes, transistors, chips. What was the switch?
cards.body: Chapter 2 finale. The machines in this chapter kept swapping one kind of switch for a better one. Line the eras up by their switch, from pins closing circuits through punched holes to transistors built into chips, and the whole story falls into place.

items.label: Holes in cards
points: A pin through a hole dips into mercury and closes a circuit

items.label: Vacuum tubes
points: Heated cathodes: hot, power-hungry, prone to burn out

items.label: Transistors, then chips
points: Small, cool and reliable, so circuits could shrink
Chips build transistors and their wiring on one piece of silicon

cards.headline: The whole chapter in one breath
cards.body: Jacquard's loom read punched cards, and Hollerith counted a census with a card per person. Babbage conceived an engine programmed with cards, and Lovelace saw it might act on things besides number. Turing's universal machine read its program from a tape. ENIAC took days of rewiring for each problem, until the Manchester Baby ran a program stored in memory. Microprocessors made personal computers affordable, and the smartphone turned a phone into a computer you can install software on.

options.label: transistors
options.rationale: The transistor came in 1947, after ENIAC.

questions.explanation: ENIAC switched with about 18,000 vacuum tubes, and lost one roughly every day or two.

questions.prompt: Put the eras of the computer's switch in order, from oldest to newest.
questions.explanation: First came holes in cards, then vacuum tubes like ENIAC's, then transistors, which were later built into chips.

questions.prompt: Every switch in this chapter was on or off. Which Chapter 1 idea is one such two-way choice?

options.label: A kilobyte
options.rationale: That's a size, many bits long.

options.label: A pixel
options.rationale: A pixel is a dot of color on a screen.

questions.explanation: A bit is one choice between two options, 1 or 0, the job every switch does.

questions.prompt: From Level 12: what did Lovelace say the Analytical Engine might act upon?

options.label: Other things besides number, even music
Cloth, like the Jacquard loom
options.rationale: She compared it to the loom, but not for weaving cloth.

questions.explanation: She wrote that it might act upon other things besides number, and might even compose music.

questions.prompt: From Level 15: what did the Manchester Baby do first, in June 1948?

options.label: Ran a program stored in its electronic memory
Put a whole processor on one chip
Replaced its vacuum tubes with transistors
options.rationale: Transistors replaced tubes in many uses only by the late 1950s.

questions.explanation: On June 21, 1948, the Baby became the first computer to run a program stored in its electronic memory.
